title: The Availability Heuristic and the Power of Review
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explains the availability heuristic — the mental shortcut where recent, easily recalled information disproportionately shapes decisions — as both a bias to guard against and a tool leaders can deliberately exploit. After noting the risk of overweighing recent examples in decision-making, the piece pivots to a practical technique: reviewing a list of vivid words or key ideas shortly before a presentation or discussion makes it more likely those words or concepts surface naturally in the moment. The author frames this as a way to intentionally load the mind's most accessible material right before a task that depends on it, turning a known cognitive bias into a genuine performance aid.
points: The availability heuristic causes decision-makers to overweigh recent, easily recalled information.
This bias can distort judgment when leaders unconsciously rely on what's freshest in memory rather than what's most relevant.
Reviewing vivid vocabulary or key ideas shortly before a presentation makes them more likely to surface naturally.
The technique works because recently reviewed material becomes more mentally 'available' during performance.
The author recommends deliberately reviewing important information right before any task that depends on it.
quotes: The Availability Heuristic is one of the mental shortcuts leaders use to make choices easier and faster.
By making these words more easily available in your mental lexicon, you will likely find you unintentionally use one or two of them during your presentation.
Any time you review information, data, working premises, insights, or language prior to an intellectual task, you make these ideas more available for use.
The Availability Heuristic is both a bias and an aid in making choices and decisions.
Make it a habit to review what is important or insightful prior to discussion or decision-making.
